label: Aug 21, 2026
headline: September 2026 Visa Bulletin (final of FY2026): Zero employment-based movement for India — EB-2 and EB-5 still unavailable, family categories explode
summary: The State Department released the September 2026 Visa Bulletin — the final bulletin of fiscal year 2026 — revealing a stark split between family-sponsored and employment-based categories. Family-sponsored categories received a year-end number dump: F3 leaped 2 years 5 months, F4 gained 2 years 2 months, F1 advanced 13 months, F2B gained 20 months, and F2A moved to August 2026 (nearly current). Employment-based categories got virtually nothing: EB-1, EB-2, EB-3, and every EB-5 line are identical to August. India EB-2 and EB-5 Unreserved remain Unavailable, EB-1 India stays frozen at October 15, 2022, and EB-3 India remains stuck at January 1, 2014. Only EB-4 and Certain Religious Workers saw minor movement. The Dates for Filing chart for employment-based categories did not change by a single day. With FY2026 ending September 30, annual limits reset October 1 — the earliest point Indian EB-2 and EB-5 applicants could see visa numbers resume. USCIS also announced a revised Form I-485 effective September 18 (aligned with the public charge rule) with no grace period for using the old version.
source: US State Department / September 2026 Visa Bulletin (Vol. XI, No. 18)

label: Aug 19, 2026
headline: Coalition sues to block Duration of Status rule before September 15 deadline — lawsuit filed in Massachusetts federal court
summary: Eight organizations representing higher education and journalism sectors filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on August 19, seeking to vacate the Duration of Status rule before it takes effect September 15. The complaint alleges DHS violated the Administrative Procedure Act by failing to conduct thorough impact analysis, not substantively responding to the nearly 22,000 negative public comments, and not considering alternative solutions to address overstay concerns. The rule replaces the 47-year-old open-ended duration of status framework with fixed four-year caps for F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors, and 240-day caps for I-visa journalists — with Chinese nationals limited to 90 days. DHS dismissed the lawsuit as performative outrage. USCIS will release revised Forms I-539 and I-765 on September 15 to align with the new rule. Indian students — the largest international student cohort in the US — face the biggest impact, particularly PhD candidates whose programs exceed four years and those relying on OPT/STEM OPT pathways. A court injunction before September 15 could delay or block implementation.
source: Reuters / Inside Higher Ed / U.S. District Court, D. Mass.

label: Aug 17, 2026
headline: August visa wait times: Kolkata B1/B2 drops to 2 months (from 7), Hyderabad work/student visas surge to 5 months — mixed signals across India consulates
summary: The State Department's August 2026 wait time data reveals a dramatic reshuffling across India's consulates. Kolkata B1/B2 visitor visa wait plunged from 210 days (7 months) in July to just 60 days (2 months), making it the fastest in the country by far. Mumbai B1/B2 improved from 300 to 255 days (8.5 months). However, Hyderabad deteriorated sharply — B1/B2 rose to 315 days (10.5 months, now the longest), while work visa (H/L/O/P/Q) waits surged from ~45 days to 150 days and student visa (F/M/J) waits tripled from 45 to 135 days. New Delhi B1/B2 held at 255 days but student visas rose to 75 days. Chennai continues showing no interview availability — only dropbox processing (1-day turnaround). The Hyderabad surge across all categories may reflect operational constraints from the expanded social media vetting mandate that hit Indian consulates in December 2025.
source: US State Department / travel.state.gov / afnovisaguide.com

label: Aug 13, 2026
headline: BIA overrules 14-year precedent: advance parole travel now triggers 3- and 10-year unlawful-presence bars
summary: In Matter of Delcarmen-Lara (29 I&N Dec. 830, BIA 2026), the Board of Immigration Appeals held that leaving the US on advance parole counts as a 'departure' for purposes of the unlawful-presence bars under INA §212(a)(9)(B). The decision expressly overrules Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly (2012), a 14-year-old precedent that immigration lawyers and DACA/TPS/I-485 applicants had relied on to travel internationally without triggering the 3-year or 10-year reentry bars. Now, anyone who accumulated 180+ days of unlawful presence and then departs on advance parole may become inadmissible — requiring an I-601 waiver to reenter. The ruling applies prospectively (trips completed before August 13 are not affected), but immigration attorneys are issuing urgent warnings not to travel on advance parole without individual legal advice. While this most directly impacts DACA recipients and TPS holders, Indian green card applicants in the lengthy EB backlog who travel on advance parole while their I-485 is pending should also review their unlawful-presence history before any international travel.
source: BIA (Matter of Delcarmen-Lara) / Murthy Law Firm / Ogletree Deakins

label: Aug 8, 2026
headline: DHS proposes eliminating 60-day grace period for H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN workers after job loss — rule sent to OMB for review
summary: The Department of Homeland Security has advanced a proposed rule (RIN: 1615-AD22) to eliminate the 60-day grace period that since 2017 has allowed H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, E-1/E-2/E-3, and TN visa holders to remain in the US for up to 60 days after employment ends to find a new sponsor, change status, or prepare to depart. The rule was sent to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) for review. If implemented, workers who lose their jobs would have to leave immediately — with no window to transfer to a new employer or file for adjustment of status. The full text has not been published yet; once OMB review concludes, it will appear in the Federal Register for 30-60 days of public comment. The grace period remains in effect during the rulemaking process. For Indian H-1B professionals — who make up over 70% of H-1B holders — the proposal would dramatically raise the stakes of any layoff, particularly during tech industry restructuring.
source: DHS / OMB-OIRA / Bloomberg Law / Ogletree Deakins

label: Aug 6, 2026
headline: Trump signs executive orders banning 'birth tourism' and expanding birthright citizenship exclusions — scrutiny may extend to student and work visas
summary: A month after the Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship 6-3, President Trump signed two new executive orders (EOs 14418 and 14419) taking a narrower approach. The first expands categories of people whose US-born children are ineligible for citizenship — including 'alien enemies,' foreign terrorist organization members, and those engaged in 'commercial transactions to purchase birthright citizenship' via surrogacy. The second bans 'birth tourism' outright, directing DOS and DHS to deny visas, revoke existing ones, and impose lifetime entry bans on foreigners suspected of traveling to the US specifically to give birth. The orders suggest scrutiny will extend beyond tourist visas to other temporary visa categories, including student and work visas. White House aide Stephen Miller declared: 'No one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a visa for this fraudulent purpose.' Legal experts say the EOs likely violate the Supreme Court's June 30 ruling; the ACLU filed to block enforcement on August 11. For Indian families on H-1B/H-4 in years-long green card queues who have US-born children, the orders raise concerns about heightened consular and port-of-entry scrutiny for pregnant visa holders — though immigration attorneys stress that having a child while on a legitimate work visa is not 'birth tourism.'
source: White House / Reuters / WSJ / CNN / ACLU

label: Aug 5, 2026
headline: USCIS can now deny H-1B, green card, and other filings without issuing a Request for Evidence — policy effective immediately
summary: USCIS updated its policy to allow officers to deny immigration applications and petitions without first issuing a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) when required initial evidence is missing or eligibility is not established. The policy applies to all requests pending or filed on or after August 5, 2026. USCIS also clarified that officers may set shorter RFE response deadlines. This means incomplete H-1B petitions, I-485 green card applications, and other filings can be denied outright — forfeiting filing fees — rather than getting a second chance to supply missing documents. For Indian applicants navigating the already-tight immigration environment, the change makes thorough, complete initial filings more critical than ever. The update rescinds the 2013-era guidance that limited denials to cases with "no possibility" of approval.
source: USCIS / Boundless Immigration

label: Jul 31, 2026
headline: Trump administration weighs $100,000 fee on OPT work permits — would target Indian students and Silicon Valley hiring pipeline
summary: The Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration is considering attaching a $100,000 fee to Optional Practical Training (OPT), the program that lets international graduates work in the US for one to three years on their student visas. About 419,000 foreign workers were on OPT in 2024. The move would effectively extend the $100K fee strategy — blocked by the First Circuit for H-1B visas — to the student-to-worker pipeline that top tech and finance firms rely on. DHS said no policy should be considered final until formally announced, but officials are discussing whether students, universities, or employers would pay. The fee would likely attach to a new requirement announced in July that forces international students to apply for a visa extension to use OPT, ending the decades-old Duration of Status framework. DHS is also working on a broader OPT regulation expected this fall. Indian students — the largest international cohort in the US — would face the biggest impact, as OPT and STEM OPT are the primary post-graduation work pathways before H-1B sponsorship.
source: Wall Street Journal / DHS

label: Jul 25, 2026
headline: First Circuit denies Trump bid to revive $100K H-1B fee — appeals court says government unlikely to win
summary: The First Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday denied the Trump administration's emergency motion to stay Judge Sorokin's June 8 ruling that struck down the $100,000 H-1B fee as an unlawful tax. The three-judge panel ruled the government has not shown it is likely to succeed on appeal, citing a 1989 Supreme Court precedent requiring clear congressional authorization for such financial burdens. The ruling means the fee is no longer enforceable — reversing the temporary stay granted by Sorokin on June 12 that had kept the fee in effect. The case (California v. Mullin, No. 26-01699) was brought by 20 Democratic-led states. Parallel challenges remain pending in California and D.C. federal courts. While the full appeal on the merits is still ahead, the First Circuit's skepticism is a strong signal. Meanwhile, Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-MT) introduced the 'End H-1B Abuse Act' in the Senate the same day, seeking to codify the $100K fee in law and bypass the constitutional objection.
source: First Circuit Court of Appeals / Reuters / Bloomberg Law / The Hindu BusinessLine

label: Jul 24, 2026
headline: Senate bill seeks 3-year H-1B visa suspension, codifies $100K fee — companion to House version escalates legislative push
summary: Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-MT) introduced the 'End H-1B Abuse Act' in the Senate, mirroring Rep. Eli Crane's April House bill. The legislation would pause all new H-1B visas for three years, permanently replace the lottery with a wage-based selection system, codify the $100,000 petition fee struck down by courts, ban concurrent employment and third-party staffing models, end the 'dual intent' provision that lets H-1B holders pursue green cards, prevent H-class visa holders from bringing dependents, bar federal agencies from sponsoring visa holders, and eliminate Optional Practical Training (OPT) for students. The bill is backed by the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR). While unlikely to pass in its current form, the Senate companion signals growing bipartisan-adjacent momentum to fundamentally reshape the H-1B program that employs hundreds of thousands of Indian tech professionals.
source: Sen. Tim Sheehy / The Hindu BusinessLine / FAIR

label: Jul 21, 2026
headline: August 2026 Visa Bulletin: Zero movement for India — EB-2 still unavailable, EB-1 and EB-3 frozen until FY2027
summary: The State Department's August 2026 Visa Bulletin, released July 21, shows no progress for Indian green card applicants across all employment-based categories. EB-2 India remains 'Unavailable' — no visas will be issued until FY2027 begins October 1. EB-1 India stays frozen at October 15, 2022. EB-3 India remains stuck at January 1, 2014 — a 12.5-year backlog. EB-5 unreserved India also remains 'Unavailable.' Meanwhile, EB-3 Rest of World advanced one month to September 1, 2024, and China EB-1 advanced to July 1, 2023. With FY2026 ending September 30, the State Department has warned that further retrogressions are possible. For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the green card queue, the bulletin confirms what many feared: no relief until the new fiscal year.
source: US State Department / August 2026 Visa Bulletin

label: Jul 16, 2026
headline: DHS publishes final rule ending 'Duration of Status' — student visas capped at 4 years, grace period halved to 30 days
summary: The Department of Homeland Security published the final rule scrapping the 47-year-old 'Duration of Status' framework for F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, and I-visa journalists. Student and exchange visas are now capped at four years maximum, with extensions requiring USCIS filing. The grace period after program completion is cut from 60 to 30 days. Graduate students are prohibited from changing educational objectives or transferring schools without authorization. Journalists get a 240-day cap (90 days for Chinese nationals). The rule takes effect 60 days after Federal Register publication, subject to congressional review. DHS Secretary Mullin said the old system 'compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud.' Indian students — the largest international cohort in the US — face the biggest impact, especially PhD candidates in programs exceeding four years. Immigration experts warn the rule will also narrow the Day 1 CPT pathway used by many Indian professionals after H-1B lottery rejections, and could deter graduate students from choosing US universities.
source: DHS / Federal Register / USA TODAY / WSJ / Washington Examiner

label: Jul 16, 2026
headline: USCIS revives 'public charge' rule — green card applicants using Medicaid, food stamps, housing vouchers face denials starting September 18
summary: DHS published a final rule rescinding the Biden-era 2022 public charge regulation and restoring the broader Trump first-term criteria. Starting September 18, 2026, USCIS officers can weigh an applicant's use of Medicaid, SNAP (food stamps), housing vouchers, and other means-tested benefits when deciding whether the applicant is likely to become a 'public charge' — a factor in green card adjudication. The Biden rule had limited consideration to only cash welfare. About 588,000 applicants undergo public charge reviews annually. USCIS will roll out a revised Form I-485 and reject older versions filed on or after September 18. USCIS Director Edlow said the agency is 'restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves.' Benefits received by family members won't count as the applicant's own, but officers may consider them when assessing finances. Immigration advocates warn of a 'chilling effect' on hundreds of thousands of immigrant families, including many Indian green card holders, who may disenroll from benefits they or their US-citizen children are eligible for to avoid jeopardizing their applications.
source: USCIS / DHS / CNN / Reuters / Daily Caller

label: Jul 15, 2026
headline: Trump administration weighs $100,000 bond for overseas green card applicants — pilot planned for select countries
summary: The State Department is developing a proposal to require some immigrant visa applicants at US consulates abroad to post a refundable bond of up to $100,000 before receiving a green card, the Wall Street Journal reported. The bond would be returned only after the applicant becomes a US citizen — a process taking at least five years — serving as collateral to ensure financial self-sufficiency. Family members could post the bond on behalf of applicants. Officials plan to pilot the program with a small number of countries before deciding on a broader rollout. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott confirmed the department is 'exploring existing authorities under the Immigration and Nationality Act' to implement the requirement. While most employment-based Indian applicants (H-1B holders already in the US) bypass overseas consular processing, a full rollout could heavily impact family-sponsored green card applicants from India. The proposal follows a similar pilot requiring tourist visa applicants from certain countries to post bonds of up to $15,000, where 97% compliance was reported.
source: Wall Street Journal / State Department / Outlook Business / DevDiscourse

label: Jul 10, 2026
headline: Trump regulatory agenda targets H-1B, H-4, OPT in sweeping overhaul — formal proposals expected August
summary: The Unified Regulatory Agendas released by DHS, DOL, and the State Department outline the most comprehensive tightening of the US immigration system in years. Key proposals: (1) H-4 EAD auto-extension ending — a final rule expected this month would end automatic work permit extensions for H-4 spouses, predominantly Indian, creating potential work authorization gaps even for timely filers; (2) Green Card wage thresholds rising from the 17th to the 34th percentile for H-1B workers and employment-based permanent residency applicants; (3) H-1B cap exemptions for universities, nonprofit research organizations, and affiliated institutions may be limited, forcing more applicants into the lottery; (4) STEM OPT extension and CPT restrictions proposed for February 2027, threatening the primary post-graduation work pathway for Indian students. None of the measures has taken effect yet, but formal proposals could open for public comment as early as August, with implementation potentially following soon after. Combined with the already-in-effect $100K H-1B fee and EB-2 India 'Unavailable' status, the regulatory agenda signals an unprecedented squeeze on Indian immigration pathways.
source: DHS / DOL / State Department Unified Regulatory Agendas / Outlook Business / Bhaskar English

label: Jul 9, 2026
headline: DOL launches major H-1B fraud investigation — dozens of subpoenas issued, Vance says 'no more'
summary: Vice President JD Vance and DOL Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced a major investigation into H-1B visa fraud at a Milwaukee event on July 8. The DOL has already issued dozens of subpoenas targeting employers and labor brokers who allegedly submitted fraudulent H-1B petitions, exploited foreign workers through wage-kickback schemes, and undercut American workers with below-market labor. D'Esposito said the fraud has cost 'hundreds of millions' in the medical industry alone, with unqualified workers placed in healthcare facilities. DHS internal reviews suggest as many as one-fifth of H-1B petitions may be fraudulent. While immigration attorneys counter that fraud is rare in practice, the probe signals intensified enforcement scrutiny on H-1B employers — particularly IT staffing firms and outsourcing companies that employ large numbers of Indian workers. Vance stated: 'If you are trying to take advantage of that visa program, you are not allowed into the United States of America.'
source: VP JD Vance / DOL Inspector General / NY Post / Milwaukee Journal Sentinel

label: Jul 6, 2026
headline: US visa wait times hit new highs at Indian consulates — Mumbai at 10 months, Kolkata nearly doubles to 7 months
summary: The State Department's July 2026 wait time data reveals further deterioration across all five Indian consulates. Mumbai B1/B2 waits have hit 300 days (10 months), the longest nationally. New Delhi jumped to 255 days (8.5 months), up from 7.5 months in June. Kolkata — previously the fastest option at 4 months — has surged to 210 days (7 months), nearly doubling in weeks. Hyderabad holds at 285 days (9.5 months). Chennai shows no interview availability at all, with only dropbox processing listed. Work visa (H/L/O/P/Q) waits remain 45–105 days depending on the consulate, and student visa (F/M/J) waits are 45–60 days. The continued surge comes despite the State Department's $750 premium interview pilot launching July 1, which offers B1/B2 applicants expedited appointments within 10 business days at select posts. Participating locations have not yet been announced for India. With the USCIS signature rule also taking effect July 10 — potentially causing denials for digital-signature filings — Indian visa applicants face a convergence of new pressures heading into the second half of 2026.
source: US State Department / travel.state.gov / afnovisaguide.com

label: Jul 1, 2026
headline: Supreme Court upholds birthright citizenship 6-3 — strikes down Trump executive order as unconstitutional
summary: In a landmark ruling on the final day of its term, the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's executive order that sought to deny automatic citizenship to children born in the US to non-citizen parents. Chief Justice Roberts, writing for a five-member majority, held that the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause — granting citizenship to all persons born on US soil and "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" — cannot be overridden by executive action, citing the 1898 precedent United States v. Wong Kim Ark. Justice Kavanaugh concurred on statutory grounds, suggesting Congress could legislate changes but the president cannot act alone. The ruling is especially significant for Indian families navigating years-long green card backlogs on H-1B, H-4, L-1, and other temporary visas, where children are frequently born in the US long before their parents obtain permanent residency. Trump called the decision "too bad for our country" and urged Congress to pass legislation ending birthright citizenship — a move that would face even steeper constitutional hurdles.
source: US Supreme Court (Trump v. Barbara) / NBC News / Brookings / Reuters

label: Jun 30, 2026
headline: USCIS signature crackdown takes effect July 10 — DocuSign and digital shortcuts may trigger denials on H-1B and green card filings
summary: An interim final rule published May 11 in the Federal Register takes effect July 10, 2026, giving USCIS explicit authority to deny — not just reject — immigration benefit requests with invalid signatures. Unlike a rejection (which refunds fees), a denial means the agency keeps the filing fee and the petitioner must start over. Affected filings include H-1B petitions, L-1 transfers, I-140 green card petitions, and I-485 adjustment of status applications. Prohibited formats now include DocuSign, Adobe Sign, copy-pasted digital signature images, rubber stamps, and typed names — only wet-ink signatures, scanned copies of wet-ink originals, and electronic signatures within USCIS-authorized online systems are accepted. Immigration attorneys warn USCIS may increasingly choose denial over rejection since denial lets the agency retain fees. Employers and HR teams using remote or digital signing workflows — common in the Indian IT sector — should audit their practices immediately before the July 10 deadline.
source: USCIS / Federal Register / Holland & Hart / Ogletree Deakins
